I'm 69 years old and I've been farming these same plots in Quzhou County my whole life. At my age, I don't have the energy to experiment with new crops or take big risks. The land here on the North China Plain is good for one thing above all: the winter wheat–summer maize rotation. I have 5 mu of flat, irrigated land, and that's exactly what I'll plant this year—5 mu of winter wheat in October, harvest it in early June, then immediately put in 5 mu of summer maize. I know this system; the buyers come to the village every year, and I can manage the labor with my son's help during the busy seasons.

For the wheat, I'll use an improved variety like Jimai 22 or something similar that the seed station recommends—it's what everyone around here grows. I'll rotary till the field before sowing, apply about 22 kg of nitrogen, 8 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu. The wheat needs water, so I'll irrigate four times: once before winter or early spring to help it overwinter, then at jointing, heading, and grain-filling if the rain doesn't come. I'll spray pesticides three times to control aphids and powdery mildew, which are always a problem.

For the maize, I'll plant a hybrid variety—maybe Zhengdan 958 or a similar high-yield hybrid. These days I don't till for the maize; I just drill the seeds directly into the wheat stubble to save time and labor. I'll put down about 20 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 6 kg potassium per mu. The maize only needs two irrigations—one at seedling stage and one at the big trumpet stage. Two pesticide sprays should handle the corn borer and armyworm. If the weather cooperates, I expect around 500 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize. That's my plan.
